doc.title: Frank Tiberi interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 30, 2022

title: New arrangers and the premiere of Countdown
summary: Herman approved arrangers' work; Tiberi introduced bassoon, Giant Steps and Countdown, played with one day's notice at Monterey.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: When you took over the group, and by the way I have to give Mr. Herman a lot of credit for being open-minded about adding new material.

That’s the greatest part of that actually, the reason why I stayed there for all of those years is because everybody came in — you take Tony Klatka, Alan Broadbent, Bill Stapleton, they all come in — they wrote what they wanted to and he would just approve it every time. And I mean Alan Vizutti, you know, the trumpet player, he’d come in with the “Fire Dance” and my tunes too. But he wasn’t there when my tunes — actually I think so, no, I don’t think he ever heard my tunes. But no, I mean you know Fedchock did a lot of arrangements also that well they were great. Everybody was doing things that they liked. And we did, you know before that the band was playing like Richard Evans’ “MacArthur Park” and all that. And then I introduced the band with a bassoon and “Giant Steps” and “Countdown.” Well the “Countdown” thing was I think at the Monterey Jazz Festival. And I wrote it for two years and I could never really get it in because everything

was planned. All the sessions were planned. But one day before, Woody comes up to me and says, “You know, Frank, we need a hot number.” I says, “Have I got a hot number for you.” And so we performed it. I wonder if you ever heard of the tune, I don’t know if you have.
Yes I have. It was like how much time did you get to rehearse it?

One day before. One day before. I mean you know why? Because we had Stan Getz there, we had Diz, we had Woody Shaw, we had Slide Hampton. Slide Hampton had three charts over there and they were doing all the soloing but the band didn’t do anything. And so that’s why he came up to me and here I am holding an arrangement that I made for two years and I went, “Do I have something hot for you.” I thought that was funny.
Had you actually heard it played before then?
Oh that’s a bit of a — I know like my charts I always hear something, oh boy I have to fix that.

No. And actually if you listen to it I’ve been using division of twelve tones, equal division of twelve tones on it actually if you really — I incorporated all that actually. I mean they were only a couple of things that I wrote but every time I wrote something as I say it was only for my solos.
